lines.t: Forty years that stone's sung me awake. Today it forgot the words.
Well. Licensing day waits for no stone. Come — three little ones have been watching the door all morning.
Don't pick the strongest. Pick the one that looks back at you.
{starter}. Good. It's chosen you back — see the ears? Treat that like a promise.
And this is your Tuning Ledger. Every kin you meet, every stone you hear — it all goes in here. Don't spill tea on it. I did. Twice.
Three Salves for scrapes. Now go on — I heard Cass stomping off toward the north lane. Loudly. As always.
Cass is waiting by the north lane with {rival_starter}, practically vibrating. Go and get it over with.
Meet me on the green by the Chordstone. I want to show you something before you go anywhere.
No — no, no. Easy, little one — !
It's the stone. They find their way by it. Without it they're lost.
The little one went north, into the dusk. And look what was left at the stone's foot — a brass survey stake.
'Service ref. 114 — Larkhollow.' Service? Nobody services a Chordstone. You *listen* to one.

options.label: I'll find out who did this.

lines.t: You brought it home. Look at it — fed, brushed, and furious about the whole business. Just like me.
It hasn't stopped staring at you since you walked in. Will you foster it? It'd go with you, not stay in my pen.
Strange visitor lately. A wild young of Cass's line has been hanging round the fosterage. Won't let anyone near.
I think it's listening for a chord. Bring your {starter}'s line and the little one's line to the Larkhollow Chordstone, and let them sing together.
Both lines in your troupe, then the Chordstone on the green. Three voices make a triad. The stone will do the rest.
A letter came. From Odile. Neat hand, like always — she used to label my screwdrivers.
She says she's listening now. Actually listening. …Put the kettle on, {player}. I need a minute.
A Keynote! Wren's, too — she still writes her letters in moss ink, you know. Unreadable.
Each one tunes a new register. Mind you listen to what it opens, not just what it wins.
No sign of the little one in the orchards. If you see small tracks heading anywhere in a hurry — follow them.
Thistledown Way's straight north. There's a Dozebud that naps by the stile most mornings. Ask it nicely.
Stuck? Check the Registers page in your Ledger. The stones always tell you what they want.
Cass will sulk for an hour and then want a rematch. Good for them. Now — come look at this.
See that carving on the bramble knots? That's a glyph. Kin who share its voice can sing to it. Go on — let {starter} try.
Hear that? The stone isn't dead. It's holding its breath. Something's pressing on it.
The oldest register of all is Rootcall — a verdant voice that coaxes roots and seed-knots. {starter} can't sing it. A verdant kin can.
Five Reed Chimes. Weaken, don't wound. A Chime asks. It doesn't grab.
Listen to the rings — one, two, three. If the third holds, you're friends. Then touch the white stone on Thistledown Way. It'll remember you.
Oriel said wait outside. So I'm waiting outside. Loudly.
Go in, go in! No — wait. Okay, go in. I'm right behind you. Not in a weird way.
Okay. Okay! First one doesn't count. That's a rule. I just made it.
I'm going north. Mum always says the road teaches faster than books. …Don't tell her I quoted her.
Ha! …Huh. That felt less amazing than I thought. Good match, {player}.
Oriel's waving at you from the green. Go on, I'll be up the road beating hedges.
Did I miss it? I missed it. Fine — I'll take *that* one. No reason. Definitely not because it'd flatten yours.
First battle, first win. For me, I mean. Ready?
Okay. Okay! First one doesn't count. That's a rule. I just made it.
Ha! …Huh. That felt less amazing than I thought. Good match, {player}.
No troupe yet, love? Then there's nothing to mend but your nerves. Oriel's expecting you — go on.
Come in out of the breeze, love. Kettle's on, bowl's warm. What'll it be?
Sit by the fire, love. There — hear that? They're in tune again.
Welcome to the Chandlery! Everything's labelled! Mostly correctly!
Hear it? Tink-a-tink. The stone may be sulking, but my eaves are singing. Thank you, {player}.
That's her! Dented, muddy, and still perfectly flat in the third tube. Exactly how I made her.
Here — for your trouble. And a few Salves. My late wife swore by them for everything, including toast.
It'll have rolled downhill to the stream on Thistledown Way. West bank, where the water bends south. Mind your boots.
My wind-chime jumped off the eaves at dawn — same moment the stone went quiet. Rolled clean out of the village.
You'll be heading up Thistledown Way? If you spot a brass chime in the stream, I'd be ever so grateful.
Fifty years I've hung that chime. It's never once jumped. Something's off with the air this morning, mark me.
The Dozebuds won't wake, not properly. They open one eye, look at the stone, and go back under. Can't blame them.
Mind the crates, there's a Dozebud asleep in the second one. And the third. The first one's just apples. Probably.
They nap in the orchard because the stone hums them to sleep. Today they're only pretending.
You got a kin?! Can I pat it? Can it do a trick? Can it carry chime-strings like the Gustlings do?
When I'm big I'm going to be a Tuner and I'm going to have ONE HUNDRED kin. Or four. Four's also good.
A Gustling flew off with a whole string of chimes this morning! It went jingle-jingle-jingle all the way over the brook.
Mum says it'll bring them back. Mum says a lot of things.
Hear that? The stone's back on pitch. I've re-strung every fiddle in the shop out of sheer joy. Customers are baffled.
Forty years I've tuned my fiddles to that stone at dawn. This morning I had to tune to the kettle. It's a B-flat. A sad one.
Luthier's rule: if a string won't hold its note, something's pulling on it. Same goes for stones, I'd wager.
Nope. Nuh-uh. Nobody goes up Thistledown Way without a kin. Oriel's orders. I'm the gate now. I'm very official.
Official gate report: you have a kin. Gate is open. Please enjoy the road and don't get eaten by a hedge.
That stake someone hammered in by the stone — brass, stamped with a number, fitted by someone who knew exactly what they were doing.
Surveyors, I'd say. I just can't think what they'd be surveying. Stones don't move. Well. Not usually.
I've been writing down the stone's hum every dawn for three years. Today's entry is just a very long dash.
Oriel says it's not broken. I say it's the most interesting thing that's ever happened in Larkhollow. We're both right.
Dawn in Larkhollow. The Chordstone on the green hums its morning note… and stops, halfway through.
Somewhere down the lane, a fosterage gate bangs open and three sets of small paws scatter.
Forty years that stone's sung me awake. Today it forgot the words.
Well. Licensing day waits for no stone. Come to my workshop, {player} — three little ones have been watching the door all morning.
